title: The Aiyar Conceived the Marriage
paragraphs: The well-meaning elders of the village Assembled at the public hall And had a brainstorming session:
“I see that youth quite often By the pond, near the river bank, In the sandy plain where horses fall over.

The young woman keeps waiting for the youth Without fail Even if the scabbard fish are not to be seen in the river, Even if the carp forget to pop up in the pond And even if the horses fail to make their visit.
Day in, day out, These two frequent under cover By the hill, off the home

In the jasmine garden, in the coconut grove, In the mango grove, in the teakwood jungle; They walk hand in hand tiptoe like shadows Speaking in hushed tones, Deceiving themselves That they do it all unknown to the village folk.
We must catch them red-handed-- The boy who comes furtively And the maid of undefiled purity-- And put an end to their clandestine love career. We must see them man and wife married.
The boy might desert the girl Despite his promise to her That he would forget her not Even if it be death to him.
A time may come When falsehood and deception would rule the day; We cannot afford to lose the girl And go about crying over it.
We must talk to them right today; We must take the matter to their parents.”
As the elders were splitting their heads thus, The lovers made their presence right before them.

The headman stately as the temple car addressed them: “See how worried the folks of the hamlet are! You keep meeting in rendezvous secret By day and by night, Near the house, by the fence And everywhere around.
How would you convince us That you would not desert the girl eventually?” Fire of rage flew from the headman’s eyes.
The boy responded, “Well said, sire! We would remain unseparated Even in the world after death. Do take it from me!”
The headman said, “The times are changing And deceit looks raising its ugly head. Let’s summon the Aiyar.”
The Aiyar appeared there forthwith Asking about the reason for the summon.
One in the assembly wondered: “Should we need the Aiyar here? He belongs to an alien caste.”

The village headman explained then: “Dear friend! He is not the Aiyar you suppose; Be it clear in your mind, He is the one venerable amongst us, The one fit to sit at the head Capable of prescribing things righteous And prohibiting ways evil.
He has conceived of marriage That would guard against Falsity and deceit in love relations.”
The Aiyar, unblemished, stood up and spoke then, “Bring here the relations of the lovers Including their parents.”
Prompt they came. “Do you consent to the union of these lovers?” Aiyar asked. They nodded their heads in approval.
“All is fine! No need for worry! The clandestine love career has come to an end. Let’s conduct the marriage called karaṇam That would be a celebration Of the love of these two.”

> In so far as > The love career of the hero and the heroine > Unfolds to be inferred in discourses private, > And in so far as > It is thrown into the subject of gossip in public, > The acts of the hero must bear the prime responsibility for it. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 48) > > The hero and the heroine > Enter into marital union > Either after their clandestine union becomes public knowledge > Or before it happens. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 49) > > Sage men there conceived solemnized wedding > When falsity and breach of trust cropped up, > So has it been said. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 4)

Note: Aiyar is an indigenous Tamil word meaning a respectable elderly person of superior virtue and worth. Here this term refers to one of Tamil antiquity. There are misinterpretations of Aiyar as being derived from ‘Aryan.’ The Aiyar formulated the marriage rites to guard against love falling into deceit and falsity. This phase of marriage had been preceded by a culture when they did not visualize the need for marriage. It is obvious that the conduct of marriage should have come into existence before the days of Tolkāppiyar. The need for marriage then might have been necessitated after the advent of the alien cultures and races.
Veḷḷaivāraṇar The History of Tolkāppiyam.
